title: The objective, not the instructions
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: When did someone give you the goal, not the instructions, and how did it feel?

Jose asked: what is the value of saying to a person: fix the problem on your own, I'm going to give you one month? Or should I say: this is the strategy, this is the direction, and give them a spoonful of direction?

A student said: it is better to give me the objective without the instructions. If you just give me instructions, it doesn't stick in my head as permanent knowledge as much as if I had to figure it out and cut the path myself.

Jose said that with the person in the book looking out of the window and asking: do you believe in it? he is empowering the other person to find the solution. I can create pressure, momentum, an environment where you have the power to make decisions, and where every day you're inspired.
On the other side of the threshold of pain, risk and decision-making you come out a different person, he said. We become leaders of greatness by pushing people to find their own solutions.
A student said: that is how you maintain momentum. When the objective isn't being hit, instead of wallowing, you look and ask: what are we doing differently now? Just take more shots.

Jose said the person's abstractions, like: let's be bold, I want the future to look like the future, are not giving solutions to people. He said he sees the leadership style changing: pushing people to make decisions more than making them himself.

A student said: that has to do with the scale of his companies getting bigger and bigger. Jose said: one hundred percent. He is not the programmer sleeping under the desk anymore. He has several companies and a lot of people to run.

Jose said he sees it as a choice: do I want successful companies, or do I want to be the one who puts out all the fires and does everything on my own and works days and nights, with no end? Or do I delegate, trust people and push them in the right direction?
A student said: it is also adopting the mindset of: make a decision, even if it's wrong. As long as you are making decisions you are maintaining momentum.

Jose said that he is being extreme: you didn't do it, there is no excuse, and as leaders we need to say that. It doesn't matter if we have a problem with this or that. He said this is his own strong view.
Which of your people could you give an objective to, and when?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write an objective you could give someone without instructions.
Write what they will learn by finding the path.
Write what pressure and environment you will create.
Write when you will delegate and stop putting out fires yourself.
Write where you would draw the line on excuses, and how you would say it.

check.q: What did a student prefer to be given?
What did a student say changes how the person leads?
What did a student say maintains momentum?
choices: Making a decision, even if it's wrong

recap: Give the objective, not the instructions. Delegate as you grow. Decide, even if you may be wrong.
